LESSONS.title: What an inference engine actually does
LESSONS.goal: Explain what happens when a model answers, and what an inference engine contributes.
LESSONS.recall: What do you think happens between sending a prompt and seeing the first word?
LESSONS.predict: If two companies serve identical weights, must their speed and running cost be identical?
layers:
Start with a question you have probably already had.

You send a message to a chatbot. There is a pause, then the answer starts appearing a little at a time. Somewhere, a computer is turning your message into an answer. What is it actually doing, and why can one service feel much faster than another?

To answer that, we need to separate three things that are often all called “the model”: the learned model itself, the software that runs it, and the service you interact with.

The model contains learned numbers.

During training, a computer adjusts a large collection of numbers so that the model gets better at predicting text. Those numbers are called weights. Think of them as the settings of a very large machine: their values determine how information moves through the machine and which predictions it makes.

After training, you can save the weights to files. When you fine-tune a base model, you adjust those learned numbers or add a smaller learned update to them. You are changing the model’s behavior.

Answering uses those numbers.

When the model answers your question, it uses its weights to calculate what piece of text could come next. It chooses one piece, adds it to the text so far, and uses the longer text to make the next prediction. Repeating that process produces a response.

Using a trained model to make predictions is called inference. In ordinary inference, the model does not update its weights after each word. Its working state changes as the conversation grows, but its learned weights stay fixed.

The engine organizes the work.

Someone must load the weights, reserve memory, decide which requests to work on together, run the calculations, and keep track of each unfinished answer. That software is an inference engine. Two engines can run the same learned model and still use different amounts of memory or take different amounts of time.

The service around the engine handles things such as signing you in, deciding which machine receives your request, and sending the answer back to your screen. A faster engine helps, but the service can add delays too.

DeepInfer is an inference engine. We will use it to study these decisions after we understand the smaller pieces. Your first job is simply to keep the learned model, the engine, and the surrounding service separate in your mind.

Follow a single request from left to right. Text first becomes a sequence of numbered pieces, which we will call tokens in lesson three. The engine feeds those numbers through the model’s calculations. The result is a set of scores for possible next pieces. The engine chooses a piece and runs the process again. Because the answer is unfinished between rounds, the engine must remember which request owns which working state.

This is why an engine is more than a function that loads a file and returns a paragraph. It coordinates a repeated process for many requests sharing limited hardware.

An engine manages execution: weight loading, memory allocation, request batching, attention state, kernels and sampling. A serving system adds routing, admission control, streaming, failures and operations.

Model quality and serving quality are separate axes. Wrong prompt formatting can make good weights look bad. Poor scheduling can make a correct model feel slow.

DeepInfer is a specialized case study. Its README currently names DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. It releases offline inference capabilities and leaves a full KV-cache service, production disaggregation and replica load balancing outside the release. That does not mean the engine lacks local attention caches.

Suppose you replace the engine but keep the same weights. What should stay the same? The answer depends on the change you are making. Some changes should reproduce the same numerical result. Others preserve the probabilities of possible outputs, even if one particular answer differs. Still others deliberately approximate the calculation to save work. Before judging speed, name which promise you are trying to keep.

Define the contract before optimizing: given weights, tokenizer, prompt IDs, attention semantics and sampling settings, what outputs are legal? Then define workload and service targets. An optimization might preserve the mathematical function, only the output distribution, or approximate both. Those are different promises.

Your long-term task is to map a bottleneck to a layer you can change, then prove both correctness and benefit. “Faster” without a workload and quality contract is an incomplete engineering statement.
example: Your team makes three changes to a chatbot. Which part of the system does each change affect?

First, the team fine-tunes the model so its replies follow your preferred writing style. That changes learned weights or a learned adapter. It belongs to the model, because it changes the prediction the same input can produce.

Next, the team arranges for the computer to process several people’s questions together. The learned weights can remain exactly the same. This is an engine decision: it changes how the computer schedules and executes the work.

Finally, the team adds a sign-in page and sends each request to an available machine. Those responsibilities belong to the surrounding service. If the chatbot feels slow, knowing which of these three parts is responsible tells you where to investigate.

options: Workload, output contract and target metrics
Only a single impressive tokens/s number

transfer: A friend asks: “If the model has already been trained, why do we still need an inference engine?” Explain the difference, then name one job the surrounding service does.

Training produced the learned numbers, or weights, that determine the model’s calculations. When the model answers, the engine repeatedly runs those calculations, chooses a next token, adds it to the text so far, and continues. It also manages memory and coordinates requests that share the hardware. The surrounding service has additional jobs, such as signing users in and sending each request to an available machine.
LESSONS.takeaway: The learned model decides which calculations to do. The engine organizes how the computer runs them.

LESSONS.title: The math you need, without the fog
LESSONS.goal: Read the small amount of arithmetic and notation that inference explanations rely on.
LESSONS.recall: What is a weight, and what changes during inference?
LESSONS.predict: Does a vector with 4 entries multiplied by a 4×6 matrix produce 4 numbers or 6?
layers:
The model works with collections of numbers.

When people explain inference, they often jump straight to words such as “tensor” and “matrix multiplication.” The underlying ideas are more concrete than the names suggest. We will start with a small example you could calculate on paper.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [2, 3]. A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers. A tensor is the general name for an array that can have one, two, or more directions of organization. A vector has one direction; a matrix has rows and columns.

A shape is a description of the container.

Suppose you have four requests, each with ten text positions, and you represent each position with six numbers. You could arrange the data in a tensor with shape [4, 10, 6]. The shape tells you the number of requests, positions, and features. It does not tell you the actual numbers stored inside.

This distinction matters when debugging. Two tensors can have the same shape and contain completely different values. A successful shape check can rule out some mistakes, but it cannot prove that a model calculated the right answer.

Multiplication mixes information.

The small calculation [2, 3] · [4, 5] means multiply matching entries and add the results: 2 × 4 + 3 × 5 = 23. This is called a dot product. Matrix multiplication repeats this idea to produce many results at once. In a model, a learned matrix transforms one collection of features into another.

You will see symbols such as [B, d]. Here B might mean the number of positions being processed and d the number of features per position. Multiplying by a matrix shaped [d, h] produces [B, h]. The matching d tells you which dimension is combined.

Always carry the units.

There is a second kind of arithmetic we will use often: “How many bytes fit?” and “How long does moving them take?” If each stored number occupies two bytes, a billion numbers take roughly two billion bytes, or two decimal gigabytes. That estimate includes those numbers only; other working memory is extra.

If a device moves one gigabyte at a rate of one hundred gigabytes per second, the transfer takes at least one hundredth of a second: ten milliseconds. Capacity answers what fits. Bandwidth answers how quickly data can move. We will use this difference to explain why very powerful hardware sometimes spends time waiting.

Read a matrix formula as a set of questions: what does each row represent, what does each column represent, and which dimension gets combined? Only then do the arithmetic. A convenient approximation counts one multiplication and one addition as two floating-point operations. That lets you estimate work without following every instruction the hardware executes.

The orientation stored by a programming library can differ from the notation in a paper. Check the declared input and output dimensions rather than assuming every weight matrix is laid out the same way.

Using row vectors: x[1,d] × W[d,h] = y[1,h]. For B tokens, X[B,d] × W[d,h] = Y[B,h]. Each output entry uses about d multiplications and d additions, so the work is about 2Bdh FLOPs.

FLOP means one floating-point operation. FLOP/s is a rate. GB is decimal bytes; GiB is 2³⁰ bytes. Bandwidth is bytes per second. Capacity is bytes. Confusing these units causes bad hardware estimates.

Logarithms turn products into sums: log(p₁p₂)=log p₁+log p₂. An average negative log probability measures how surprised the model is by known target tokens.

Some symbols describe work, while others describe a rate. A FLOP counts one arithmetic operation; FLOP/s counts how many such operations a device can perform per second. Dividing work by a rate gives time. Similarly, dividing bytes by bytes per second gives time. If the units do not cancel to the quantity you want, pause before trusting the answer.

Check dimensions before algebra. If W maps d input features to h output features, its orientation depends on the library: PyTorch linear layers store [h,d] and effectively use the transpose for row-vector input.

A gradient tells training how changing a parameter changes loss. Inference usually disables gradient tracking; it does not need backward activations or optimizer state. Do not estimate inference memory using a training multiplier.

Stable softmax subtracts the largest logit before exponentiating. The result is mathematically unchanged, but intermediate values avoid overflow. Numerical representation is part of actual execution.
example: A weight table has 10 rows and 20 columns. Each number takes two bytes. How much storage does the table need?
Count the entries first. There are 10 × 20 = 200 numbers. This is an example of using the shape to find how many values exist; you do not need to inspect the values themselves.
Multiply the entry count by the storage per entry: 200 × 2 = 400 bytes. This is the storage for the table’s raw numbers. A program may need additional memory for bookkeeping or temporary results.

Now imagine moving 400 bytes over a connection rated at 100 bytes per second. Even with no overhead, that takes four seconds. The calculation is bytes divided by bytes per second, so its result is seconds. That is the same reasoning we will later apply to billions of model weights.

questions.hint: Track tokens on rows and output features on columns.

options: 2 GB for the entire service including every cache

questions.hint: What memory has the calculation omitted?

transfer: Explain the difference between how much memory a device has and how quickly it can move data. Use a small example.
Separates capacity from transfer rate
Names bytes/s as bandwidth
Explains why both constrain inference

Capacity tells me how much data fits at once. Bandwidth tells me how many bytes can move per second. A table containing 200 numbers at two bytes each needs 400 bytes of raw storage. If a connection moves 100 bytes per second, moving that table takes at least four seconds. Having enough room to store the table does not make that transfer instant.
LESSONS.takeaway: A tensor shape tells you how numbers are arranged. Units tell you what a calculation actually measures.

LESSONS.title: Tokens, logits and choosing what comes next
LESSONS.goal: Follow the repeated choices that turn a prompt into a generated response.
LESSONS.recall: How is a probability different from an arbitrary numerical score?
LESSONS.predict: If you raise temperature, do you add knowledge or change how the same scores are sampled?
layers:
The model does not work directly on words.

Before the computer runs the model, a piece of software breaks your text into smaller pieces and assigns each piece an integer. That software is the tokenizer. The pieces are called tokens, and their integers are token IDs.

A token might represent a common word, part of a word, a punctuation mark, or a special marker. For example, a made-up tokenizer could split “unhelpful” into “un,” “help,” and “ful.” That is an illustration, not a claim about how a particular model splits that word. The exact split depends on the tokenizer.

This is why a limit of a thousand tokens is not the same as a limit of a thousand words. It is also why you need the correct tokenizer when you load a fine-tuned model: its weights were learned using particular token IDs.

One calculation produces many possible next pieces.

Suppose the input ends with “The sky is”. The model produces a numerical score for each token it could put next. Some continuations get higher scores than others. These raw scores are called logits. They are not yet probabilities and do not have to add up to one.

A calculation called softmax turns those scores into probabilities. A probability describes how likely a choice is: all the possible next-token probabilities together add up to one.

The engine still has to choose.

One way to choose is to take the token with the highest score every time. This is greedy decoding. Another way is to draw a token according to the probabilities. A less likely token can then be chosen, just as a coin can land on either side even if one side is more likely.

Temperature changes how concentrated those probabilities are. Lower temperature gives the highest-scoring choices more of the probability. Higher temperature spreads it more widely. You are changing the choice rule, not teaching the model new facts.

The chosen token becomes part of the next input.

After choosing a token, the engine adds it to the sequence so far. The model then scores what could follow that longer sequence. This matters: choosing “blue” creates a different situation from choosing “clear,” so later predictions can differ too.

Repeat the score, choose, and append cycle until a stopping condition is reached. The response on your screen is the result of those repeated choices, rather than a complete paragraph retrieved in one operation.

In the formula below, z means the raw scores and T means temperature. Dividing by a smaller positive T makes differences between scores larger before softmax converts them to probabilities. The denominator adds the exponential scores of every candidate so the final probabilities sum to one.

You do not need to memorize the formula yet. Be able to explain what changes and what stays fixed: the scores came from the model, while temperature and candidate filtering belong to the selection process.

For logits z and temperature T > 0: pᵢ=exp(zᵢ/T)/Σⱼ exp(zⱼ/T). Lower temperature concentrates probability. Greedy decoding is the limiting argmax behavior, usually implemented as a separate branch.

Top-k keeps k candidates. Top-p keeps a probability-mass prefix after sorting. Filtering and temperature order matter; record the actual engine configuration when comparing results.

A causal model represents P(x₁…xₙ)=ΠₜP(xₜ|x<ₜ). Already known prompt tokens can be evaluated together, but generated tokens depend on prior choices.

To compare two engines, giving them the same visible question is not enough if they turn it into different token IDs. Even with matching IDs, a different sampling rule can produce a different continuation. A useful debugging comparison controls the inputs and choices so you can find where the calculations first disagree.

A seed controls pseudorandom draws, not every numerical detail of the model. Reordered floating-point reductions may alter logits; a tiny change can alter an argmax or a sampled token and then the rest of the sequence.

Teacher forcing feeds a known continuation instead of feeding the model’s own outputs. It lets you compare next-token log probabilities at identical prefixes even when two generators would diverge. This is a powerful correctness tool.
example: The model assigns probabilities of 66.5%, 24.5%, and 9% to three possible next tokens. What happens next?
Under greedy decoding, the engine chooses the first token because 66.5% is the largest probability. It does not need to make a random draw to decide this.
Under sampling, the first token is most likely, but either of the other two can still be drawn. Getting the second token is therefore not, by itself, evidence that the engine made a mistake.

Whichever token is chosen gets added to the sequence. The next prediction is made using that updated sequence. Raising temperature changes the probability distribution for the choice; it does not edit the model’s learned weights.

questions.prompt: Temperature changes…
questions.why: It rescales logits at sampling time. Generation repeatedly scores possible next tokens, chooses one, and adds it to the text so far.
questions.hint: Which part happens after the model computes its scores?

questions.prompt: Why can’t ordinary autoregressive generation choose 100 unknown future tokens independently in one step?
options: All GPUs forbid matrices with 100 rows
questions.why: Future conditional distributions depend on earlier generated tokens. Speculation proposes candidates and verifies them.
questions.hint: Known text and unknown text have different dependencies.

questions.prompt: Two engines diverge on the 20th generated token. A useful next check is…
options: Teacher-force the same prefixes and compare logits
Increase temperature until the text looks similar
questions.why: A shared trajectory isolates numerical/model differences before divergent histories confound the comparison.
questions.hint: Keep the input to the comparison identical.

transfer: Explain how a model goes from a prompt to a longer answer. Include where choosing the next token happens.
Describes turning text into token IDs
Explains scoring, choosing, and appending a next token
Explains why the chosen token affects the next prediction

The tokenizer turns the prompt into numbered pieces. The model calculates scores for possible next tokens, and the engine’s selection rule chooses one. That token is added to the sequence before the next prediction is made, so each choice affects later inputs. The tokenizer and stop markers must match what the model expects. Changing temperature changes the choices, rather than changing the learned weights.
LESSONS.takeaway: Generation repeatedly scores possible next tokens, chooses one, and adds it to the text so far.

LESSONS.title: A transformer pass and its KV cache
LESSONS.goal: Explain how a new token uses earlier text, and what the engine remembers to avoid repeating work.
LESSONS.recall: What makes a generated token depend on earlier ones?
LESSONS.predict: If you retain old keys and values, do you still need to compare a new query with them?
layers:
A token needs the surrounding text to make sense.

Consider “The trophy would not fit in the suitcase because it was too large.” Working out what “it” refers to requires information from other parts of the sentence. A model needs a way for the representation of one position to use information from other positions.

Attention is one mechanism for doing that. First, the model represents each token with a list of numbers, called an embedding. It then repeatedly transforms and mixes these representations through a stack of layers. A layer is one stage of the model’s calculation.

Attention makes a weighted mixture.

For a position being processed, the model calculates three kinds of numerical representations. A query is compared with keys from visible positions to produce matching scores. Those scores determine how to mix the corresponding values. A high score means that position contributes more to the mixture.

The names can sound human, but no literal question or dictionary lookup is involved. These are lists of numbers made by multiplying learned matrices. The query/key/value vocabulary tells us which role each list plays in the calculation.

When a model is trained to continue text, a position must not read the future answer. A causal mask enforces that rule by preventing attention to later positions. The computation for an earlier position therefore does not need to change just because you append a new token.

That creates an opportunity to save work.

Suppose the engine has processed “The sky is” and is now working on the next piece. It has already calculated keys and values for the earlier positions. Instead of calculating those same representations again, it can keep them in memory.

That saved state is called a KV cache: K for keys, V for values. The new position still needs its own calculations, and its query still needs to use the relevant saved keys and values. Caching removes repeated work; it does not remove the need to read the earlier context.

The saved state belongs to a specific history.

The word “bank” in a sentence about a river can develop a different representation from “bank” in a sentence about money. Deeper layers incorporate context. You cannot generally reuse a key or value merely because the same token ID appears somewhere else.

This gives us a concrete engine responsibility: remember the right state for each request, use it in the right order, and release it when it is no longer needed. A mistake here can produce wrong predictions even while every array has a perfectly valid shape.

The attention equation below describes the comparison-and-mixture process in compact form. Multiplying queries by transposed keys produces one score for each visible query/key pair. Softmax turns those scores into mixture weights. Multiplying by the values produces the mixed representation.

During an initial prompt pass, many queries are known at once. During generation, the next query arrives as the sequence grows. The saved keys and values let both paths represent the same causal computation without repeating all earlier work.

For one head: Q=XWq; K=XWk; V=XWv, then A=softmax(QKᵀ/√d + causal_mask)V. Multiple heads run different learned projections. A residual connection adds a layer’s input back to its output; normalization stabilizes scales.

Prefill computes many positions with a triangular mask. Decode computes a new position, appends its K/V, and attends to the prefix. Cache entries depend on layer, position and preceding context; a text token alone does not identify a reusable KV value.

Cache state belongs to a request (and model identity), not globally to the token ID.

The most useful first cache test uses two ways of calculating the same thing. One path recomputes the whole prefix. The other processes it incrementally while saving K/V. Compare their numerical outputs after every position. If they disagree, you have an execution problem that you can investigate before judging whether the generated prose looks convincing.

With conventional full attention, cache reuse avoids repeated prefix projections and feed-forward work, but attention for each new query still scales with visible prefix length. KV caches trade capacity and bandwidth for saved recomputation.

For correctness, compare full-prefix forward outputs to incremental outputs at every position, including after a long prefill. Test two independent requests interleaved; accidental shared cache state can pass single-request tests.

The CPU workshop implements a tiny real causal attention block. It deliberately omits production positional schemes, multiple heads and normalization so the cache mechanism stays inspectable.
example: The prompt contains tokens A, B, and C. You now process token D. What can the engine reuse?
The engine already has saved keys and values for A, B, and C at each relevant layer. Keep those entries in the request’s cache. You do not need to rebuild them simply because D has arrived.

Calculate D’s query, key, and value. D’s query compares with the visible keys, including D’s own key, and uses the corresponding values to produce its attention result. The earlier cache is still being read.

Append D’s key and value to the saved state so the next position can use them. If the engine accidentally reads another request’s cache or puts D in the wrong position, the result can be wrong even though the cache length looks reasonable.

questions.prompt: A KV cache primarily saves…
options: Recomputing earlier positions’ keys and values
questions.why: New queries still attend to cached context. The engine saves earlier attention state so each new token can use it without rebuilding it.
questions.hint: Saved computation does not mean zero reads.

questions.prompt: Can the same text token use the same KV vector in any sentence?
options: Yes, keys depend only on spelling
No, hidden states depend on context and position
questions.why: Later-layer representations reflect preceding tokens and position.
questions.hint: The token embedding is only the start of the computation.

questions.prompt: Strongest direct cache check?
options: Full-forward and incremental logits agree on the same prefixes
The cache has the expected Python type
questions.why: Numerical equivalence across positions tests the actual computation.
questions.hint: Compare a reference computation, not the appearance of the result.

transfer: Walk through what the engine does when one new token arrives. What does it calculate, and what can it reuse?
Computes a new query/key/value
Uses past keys and values
Appends request-specific state

The new position needs its own query, key, and value. Its query uses the visible keys to work out how to mix the corresponding values. Keys and values for the earlier positions can be reused from this request’s cache instead of being recalculated. The engine then appends the new key and value. It still reads earlier state, and it must use the state from the correct history.
LESSONS.takeaway: The engine saves earlier attention state so each new token can use it without rebuilding it.

LESSONS.title: Prefill, decode and what users feel
LESSONS.goal: Separate the wait before an answer starts from the speed at which it continues.
LESSONS.recall: Why are known prompt tokens different from unknown generated tokens?
LESSONS.predict: A huge prompt gives a long initial pause but fast streaming. Which phase should you investigate first?
layers:
“The model is slow” can describe two different experiences.

You send a question and wait several seconds before anything appears. Once the answer starts, it arrives quickly. In another service, the answer begins almost immediately but then trickles out painfully slowly. Those symptoms can have different causes.

Inference engines usually distinguish prefill from decode. Prefill processes the text that is already known: your prompt. Decode continues the sequence by generating new tokens.

The prompt is already on the page.

All prompt tokens are available before the model starts answering. A well-organized computation can process many of those positions together while preserving the rule that a position must not read future positions. This builds the attention state that generation will reuse.

For ordinary generation, the later answer tokens are not known yet. The engine chooses a token, uses it to continue the calculation, and repeats. That dependency makes the work behave differently from processing the known prompt.

Measure the experience you want to improve.

Time to first token, often shortened to TTFT, measures how long it takes for the first generated token to arrive within the chosen measurement boundary. A high value can come from waiting in a queue, preparing the input, processing the prompt, or delivering the result.

Inter-token latency measures the gaps between generated tokens. People also call it time between tokens. It describes how smoothly the answer continues after it begins.

Throughput measures total work completed per second across requests. A server answering a hundred people can have high total throughput while each person still gets a slow answer. Always ask whether a number describes one user or the whole system.

Use a symptom to choose the next measurement.

If a long document causes a long initial pause but fast streaming, investigate prompt processing and everything before it first. If the initial response is quick but later tokens are slow, inspect generation. These are starting points, not proofs: queueing and network delays can also affect what a user sees.

When you later evaluate an engine for your fine-tuned model, record both the initial wait and the streaming speed. One attractive tokens-per-second number will not tell you the whole experience.

Break a request into timed stages instead of treating it as one opaque duration. A useful timeline has queue wait, input preparation, prefill, the first output, and later output gaps. State where your clock starts and ends. A timing taken inside an engine will omit some delays that a browser user experiences.

For a complete answer with ten tokens, there is one initial wait and nine later gaps. Counting ten gaps would add a delay that did not occur.

A useful decomposition is TTFT ≈ queue + preprocessing + prefill + first-sample + delivery. Total generation time is roughly TTFT plus the gaps for the remaining tokens. Decode work and prefill can compete if placed on the same accelerator.

Continuous batching admits and removes requests between steps rather than waiting for a whole fixed batch to finish. Chunked prefill splits long prompt work into budgets so it can coexist more smoothly with decode.

Prefill is often compute-heavy and low-batch decode often bandwidth-heavy. Treat that as a starting hypothesis; context length, architecture and load can change the limiting resource.

Average latency can hide users who wait much longer. A percentile such as p99 identifies a value that 99% of measured observations are at or below. If the service is overloaded, those long waits can grow even when the GPU’s own calculation time changes very little. This is why load and arrival patterns belong in an online benchmark.

Measure p50, p95 and p99, not just means. Under saturation, queueing can dominate even if device step time barely changes. A benchmark that increases batch size while ignoring request arrivals cannot characterize an online service by itself.

Define goodput explicitly: useful completed tokens or requests that meet your quality and latency criteria per second. The exact definition is a product decision. Compare configurations at a matched latency constraint, not just at their highest offline throughput.
example: The first token arrives after 400 milliseconds. Nine more tokens arrive with 50 milliseconds between them. When is the answer complete?

Count the initial wait once: the first token is already present at 400 milliseconds. That time may include queueing, input preparation, and model execution, depending on where the measurement started.
There are nine gaps after that first token. Nine times 50 milliseconds is 450 milliseconds. Those gaps describe the continuation of the answer rather than the initial wait.
Add the two parts: 400 + 450 = 850 milliseconds. A change that reduces only the initial wait affects a different part of this total from a change that shortens every later gap.

questions.prompt: Long initial pause, then quick streaming. First metric?
questions.why: The symptom concerns time until the first token. Processing the known prompt and generating the unknown continuation are different kinds of work.
questions.hint: Match the metric to the experience.

questions.prompt: 100 requests each get 10 tokens/s. Aggregate output rate?
questions.why: Aggregate throughput sums per-request rates: 100×10.
questions.hint: Per-user and fleet metrics use different denominators.

questions.prompt: Offline throughput improves while online p99 worsens. Is that possible?
options: Yes, batching or queueing can raise tail latency
questions.why: The optimization objective and arrival process differ.
questions.hint: What happens to a request waiting to join work?

transfer: Someone says their chatbot is slow. What would you ask and measure before choosing a fix?
Separates initial delay and streaming gaps
Includes queueing/preprocessing
Requests workload and percentile measurements

I would ask whether the delay comes before the first token or between later tokens. The initial wait can include queueing, input preparation, and prompt processing. Later gaps concern continued generation, but delivery delays may matter too. I would measure those stages under the person’s actual input lengths and request load, including slow requests rather than only an average. That tells me where to investigate first.
LESSONS.takeaway: Processing the known prompt and generating the unknown continuation are different kinds of work.

activity.title: Measure the wait a user actually sees.
activity.intro: A request waits in a queue for 120 milliseconds. Input preparation, prompt processing, and first-token delivery take another 180 milliseconds. The answer contains five output tokens, with 40 milliseconds between successive tokens. Use the moment the request was submitted as time zero.

fields.label: How many milliseconds until the first output token arrives?
fields.why: The initial wait includes both the queue and the work before first delivery: 120 + 180 = 300 milliseconds.

fields.label: How many milliseconds until the fifth and final output token arrives?
fields.why: After the first token there are four gaps, not five: 300 + 4 × 40 = 460 milliseconds.

activity.conclusion: A timing recorded only inside the engine can omit the queue and delivery. Save the clock boundary along with the number whenever you measure your own model.

LESSONS.title: Why GPUs wait: memory, math and kernels
LESSONS.goal: Explain why an expensive GPU can wait for data instead of doing useful arithmetic.
LESSONS.recall: How do capacity and bandwidth differ?
LESSONS.predict: If weights take 8 ms to read but arithmetic takes 1 ms, will twice the arithmetic speed halve the step?
layers:
Fast arithmetic is only useful when the numbers are available.

A GPU is a processor designed to perform many numerical operations in parallel. Language models contain a great deal of arithmetic, so GPUs can be useful for running them. But the arithmetic units cannot work on numbers they have not received yet.

Model weights and working state live in memory. During execution, data must move from that memory to the parts of the device doing calculations. Some results must then be written back. That movement takes time.

Separate fitting from moving.

Memory capacity tells you how much data can fit. Memory bandwidth tells you how many bytes can move per second. A model can fit comfortably in memory and still run slowly because each step must move a lot of data.

You will often see HBM, meaning high-bandwidth memory: the GPU’s large memory store. There is also smaller, faster storage closer to its arithmetic units. Engine developers try to arrange calculations so useful data stays close to where it is needed.

Ask which cost is setting the pace.

Imagine an operation that needs eight milliseconds to fetch its data but only one millisecond to do its arithmetic. Giving it twice as much arithmetic speed does not make the eight-millisecond transfer disappear. The operation is limited mainly by data movement.

Now imagine enough work is grouped together that the same fetched weights can be used repeatedly. More arithmetic gets done for each byte moved. This can make better use of the arithmetic units, until some other cost becomes the main limit.

A kernel is the device program doing the work.

At the implementation level, an engine calls kernels: programs that perform particular GPU operations. A better kernel might avoid writing an intermediate result to slow memory, arrange data more effectively, or combine small operations.

Using fewer bytes per stored number can help too. That is one purpose of quantization, which represents values in a more limited format. It also introduces questions about rounding, model quality, and whether the hardware has an efficient implementation.

When you hear “this optimization makes inference faster,” ask which cost it removes. Then check whether that cost actually dominates your workload. Saving memory capacity and reducing execution time are related possibilities, but they are different measurements.

A roofline calculation is a quick way to compare two limits. Divide the arithmetic work by the device’s arithmetic rate. Separately, divide the bytes that must move by the available bandwidth. Even with perfect overlap, the operation cannot finish before the larger of those two times.

This gives a lower bound under stated assumptions, not a promise about a real GPU. Additional launches, communication, temporary results, and imperfect scheduling can make actual execution slower.

A lower bound with ideal overlap is time ≥ max(FLOPs / compute_rate, bytes / bandwidth). Without overlap, costs may add. Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. Batching can reuse weights across tokens and increase this ratio.

Fusion combines operations to reduce launches and intermediate memory traffic. Tiling works on chunks that fit fast memory. FlashAttention is important prior art for reducing attention memory traffic; exact attention need not materialize the full score matrix in HBM.

Quantization stores or computes values in a reduced representation. It can lower traffic and storage, but requires suitable kernels and a quality check.

A useful optimization report connects an observed delay to a specific resource. For example, a trace might show many small kernels separated by launch gaps, suggesting a different problem from a long kernel already saturating memory bandwidth. Profile the actual operation before deciding that a new numerical format or more hardware will help.

A roofline bound is not a measured prediction. Real kernels have layouts, occupancy limits, padding and imperfect reuse. A narrower format does not guarantee a speedup if dequantization or unsupported kernels dominate.

For a dense projection, approximate work per token is 2P FLOPs for P participating weights. An MoE has active and total weights; a single dense-model memory estimate can mislead. Profile actual traffic and per-expert batch sizes.

DeepInfer integrates specialized kernel libraries. Judge each on its actual operator, precision and target hardware rather than treating “custom kernel” as evidence of an end-to-end win.
example: A toy operation reads 8 GB at 1,000 GB per second, and its arithmetic takes 1 millisecond. What is the main limit?
Calculate the transfer time: 8 divided by 1,000 is 0.008 seconds, or 8 milliseconds. Keep bytes and bytes per second in matching units so the result is a time.

Compare that with the one millisecond of arithmetic. Even if the two activities overlap perfectly, the operation takes at least the larger time: 8 milliseconds. With less overlap or extra overhead, it can take longer.

Doubling the arithmetic speed changes one millisecond to half a millisecond, while the eight-millisecond transfer remains. Reducing data traffic or using the same fetched data for more work is a more promising direction under these assumptions.

questions.prompt: Faster math units help least when…
questions.why: Improving a non-limiting resource cannot remove the limiting cost. Execution time can be limited by moving data, doing arithmetic, or coordinating the work.
questions.hint: Compare the two time estimates.

questions.prompt: 8 GB / 1 TB per second equals…
questions.why: Use consistent decimal units: 8/1000 s.
questions.hint: A TB is 1,000 GB here.

questions.prompt: Why can fusion help without reducing mathematical FLOPs?
options: It changes all probabilities to zero
It can remove intermediate writes and launch overhead
It trains a smaller model automatically
questions.why: Execution costs include moving intermediate results and dispatching work.
questions.hint: Math count is only one budget.

transfer: A teammate suggests using a smaller numerical format to speed up your endpoint. What would you want to know before adopting it?
Identifies limiting operation and resource
Checks hardware/kernel support
Tests numerical/task quality and end-to-end latency

I would first find which operation and resource are taking the time. Fewer stored bytes may help if data movement is the limit, but it will not automatically fix a scheduling delay or an inefficient conversion step. I would check hardware and kernel support, compare results with a reference, and evaluate task quality. Then I would repeat the same workload to see whether user-visible latency actually improves.
LESSONS.takeaway: Execution time can be limited by moving data, doing arithmetic, or coordinating the work.

activity.title: Choose which limit to investigate first.
activity.intro: For one toy operation, the amount of arithmetic divided by the arithmetic rate gives 2 milliseconds. Moving the needed data at the available bandwidth gives 8 milliseconds. Assume ideal overlap between the two. This is an estimate for one operation, not a measured whole-model latency.

fields.label: What is the ideal lower bound in milliseconds?
fields.why: With ideal overlap, the lower bound is the larger cost: max(2, 8) = 8 milliseconds.

fields.label: Which limit dominates this estimate?
options: The rate at which data can move
fields.why: The data movement takes longer than the arithmetic under these assumptions. Faster arithmetic alone would leave the 8-millisecond limit.

fields.label: Which observation would best test whether that estimate describes a real run?
options: Only the advertised peak arithmetic rate
A runtime trace showing where time and data movement go
fields.why: A trace can expose actual waiting, transfers, and execution. The toy estimate is a hypothesis about the limiting resource, not evidence that a real run reaches that limit.

activity.conclusion: Use a simple estimate to choose a question for the profiler. Let the observed execution determine the change you try.

LESSONS.title: Batching and overlapping CPU with GPU work
LESSONS.goal: Explain how serving requests together can save work, and why it can still make someone wait.
LESSONS.recall: Why can reusing the same weights across requests improve arithmetic intensity?
LESSONS.predict: If one request finishes early in a fixed batch, must its slot stay empty?
layers:
A server usually has more than one person to answer.

Suppose ten people are using the same model. Their questions and conversation histories differ, but the model’s weights can be the same. Rather than execute each request completely separately, an engine can organize some of their calculations together.

This is called batching. It can spread setup costs over more work and let the hardware use the same model weights for multiple positions. Larger groups can also turn small numerical operations into larger ones that the GPU handles more efficiently.

The requests still have separate lives.

One person may ask for a short answer while another requests a long report. If you start with a fixed group and keep it unchanged until everybody finishes, the short request can leave an unused place while the long one continues.

Continuous batching lets the active group change between execution steps. When a request finishes, another waiting request can take its place. This can keep the hardware busier without pretending the requests share one conversation.

The engine’s scheduler decides which work runs in each step. It must respect memory limits and decide how to divide attention among short prompts, long prompts, and responses that are already streaming.

The CPU can also make the GPU wait.

The CPU is the general-purpose processor running much of the engine’s coordination code. It prepares work, launches GPU operations, and handles results. If the GPU finishes and then waits while the CPU prepares the next step, arithmetic capacity sits unused.

Some of that work can overlap. While the GPU runs one step, the CPU may be able to prepare safe parts of a later step. This is one reason engines use asynchronous execution: they avoid waiting earlier than a dependency requires.

More efficiency does not mean every request gets faster.

A larger group can take longer to process as a whole. A request might also wait for other work to join its batch. Total output per second can improve even while an individual user experiences a longer delay.

So a good scheduler is making a tradeoff under actual demand. To judge it, inspect both the amount of useful work completed and the waits experienced by individual requests.

Think of CPU and GPU work as two lanes on a timeline. Without overlap, the second lane stays empty while the first prepares a step. With overlap, preparation for a future step can happen while current device work runs. The important question is whether the future preparation needs results that do not exist yet.

Moving independent work earlier is safe. Reading an unfinished result, or reusing memory that an unfinished operation still needs, is not.

A serial round might spend 2 ms scheduling, 8 ms executing and 1 ms handling results: 11 ms. If dependencies allow CPU work for a future round to overlap current GPU work, steady-state gaps can shrink. Startup and draining still cost time.

The word asynchronous does not remove dependencies. It moves safe work earlier and waits only when a result is actually needed. Speculative scheduling must handle requests that finish or reject drafts after future work is prepared.

In DeepInfer, follow the engine’s async execution path and worker state rather than inferring behavior from the “zero-overhead” label.

A copy that looks wasteful may protect the lifetime of data. If an engine returns a view into a reusable buffer, a later step can overwrite that buffer while earlier results still refer to it. Before removing a copy, identify who owns the bytes and when every consumer has finished reading them.

Watch for ownership: an output buffer cannot be reused while a consumer still reads it. Deferred releases, events and pinned host buffers can be correctness mechanisms, not clutter. Preserve command ordering when changing overlap.

A good change includes a timeline or trace showing the removed idle period, plus tests for early stop, cancellation and different sequence lengths. GPU utilization alone does not show which requests benefit.
example: A batch contains a short answer and a long answer. The short answer finishes first. What should the engine do with its place?
First, notice that the finished request no longer needs future model steps. Its request-owned state can be released when nothing still uses it. The long answer still needs its own separate state.

With a fixed batch, the engine might leave the short request’s place unused until the whole group finishes. With continuous batching, it can admit a waiting request between steps and give that new request its own state.

Now measure the result. Reusing the place can improve overall throughput, but the waiting request still has an initial delay and each step still has a duration. Check those times before claiming every user received a faster answer.

questions.prompt: Continuous batching lets you…
options: Share one request’s private history with everyone
questions.why: The active set can change as individual requests finish. Batching shares execution costs; scheduling decides whose work gets those benefits and when.
questions.hint: Which unit finishes independently?

questions.prompt: Larger batches always improve individual latency.
options: False: step duration and waiting may increase
questions.why: More work per step can improve aggregate efficiency while slowing an individual request.
questions.hint: Distinguish amortization from latency.

questions.prompt: An async rewrite reuses a buffer before its prior output is consumed. Main concern?
options: Data corruption from a lifetime/dependency error
questions.why: Overlapping work changes when memory can safely be reused.
questions.hint: Who still owns a reference to those bytes?

transfer: Explain one useful way for CPU work and GPU work to overlap, and one moment when the engine must still wait.
Shows two execution resources
Names the data dependency causing a wait
Includes startup or draining cost

The CPU can prepare independent metadata for a future step while the GPU calculates the current step. That avoids making the GPU wait unnecessarily afterward. But the CPU must wait before reading results that have not finished, and it cannot safely release or overwrite buffers still in use. There is also initial setup before the pipeline fills. Overlap changes the timing of safe work; it does not remove its dependencies.
LESSONS.takeaway: Batching shares execution costs; scheduling decides whose work gets those benefits and when.

LESSONS.title: KV memory, paging and prefix reuse
LESSONS.goal: Distinguish keeping a request’s state, organizing its memory, and reusing another request’s prefix.
LESSONS.recall: What computation does a KV cache avoid, and what work remains?
LESSONS.predict: If two prompts share the same first 1,000 tokens, can that prefix be reused when their model weights differ?
layers:
“Caching” describes several different ideas here.

You have already seen a KV cache: saved attention state from earlier positions in a request. As the answer grows, that saved state grows too. Keeping it avoids rebuilding earlier keys and values at every generation step.

Once you serve many requests, two more questions arise. How should the engine allocate space for growing sequences? And can a new request reuse work that an earlier request already did?

Paging answers the allocation question.

If every request needed one large continuous stretch of memory, growing and shrinking requests could leave awkward gaps. An engine can instead divide state into blocks and keep a map from a request’s logical positions to its allocated blocks.

This is paging. The idea resembles using numbered storage blocks rather than demanding that every file occupy one uninterrupted region. The main benefit is organizing memory and sharing compatible blocks more flexibly.

Prefix reuse answers the repeated-work question.

Suppose many requests begin with exactly the same long instructions. An engine may be able to reuse the saved state for that common beginning instead of processing it again. This is prefix caching. A prefix is simply the shared beginning of a sequence.

The word “exactly” matters. The raw text, its token IDs, and the model settings must describe a compatible computation. Changing an adapter can change the keys and values even if the prompt text stays the same.

Saved work has to outweigh the price of getting it back.

A reused prefix might live on another machine. Looking it up, transferring it, and attaching it to the new request can take time. If recomputing the prefix would have been quicker, a cache hit can actually increase the user’s wait.

That is why hit rate alone is incomplete. It tells you how often stored work was found, not whether retrieving it improved the service.

Memory grows with the amount of live context.

More requests and longer histories generally mean more retained attention state. In a conventional cache, doubling both the number of requests and their context lengths makes the raw state four times larger. The exact storage formula depends on the model’s attention design; compressed designs do not necessarily use the conventional layout.

In the storage formula below, count keys and values separately, then multiply by layers, requests, positions, KV heads, head dimensions, and bytes per value. “Heads” are separate attention projections; some architectures share fewer key/value heads among more query heads. This sharing changes the amount of retained state.

The formula estimates raw entries only. It leaves out temporary working memory, allocation bookkeeping, and unused capacity inside partially filled blocks.

For a conventional uncompressed cache: bytes = 2 × layers × batch × tokens × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element. The 2 counts K and V. This formula excludes allocator overhead and is not a V4.1 cache estimate.

Grouped-query attention (GQA) shares fewer KV heads among query heads. Multi-query attention uses one KV head. These are model-architecture choices, distinct from allocating KV pages.

Prefix reuse needs a hit, retrieval, transfer and state attachment. A saved prefill can be outweighed by a slow remote fetch. Cache hit rate alone is incomplete.

Cache correctness is a compatibility problem. A useful test deliberately keeps the prompt fixed while changing an attention-affecting adapter. The second request must behave like an uncached computation under its own adapter, not like a mixture of the two models. Testing only that a lookup succeeds would miss the underlying error.

Correct reuse requires matching weights, adapter, tokenization, positional settings, attention semantics and compatible representation. Adapter changes can invalidate cached hidden state even if the raw prompt is unchanged. A new turn can reuse only the common valid prefix.

Test cache boundaries: lengths just below/at/above a block, cache eviction during activity, request cancellation and reusing the same prompt under different adapters. Separate allocation correctness from content correctness.

The engine’s local cache allocator and a persistent fleet-wide cache service solve different problems. Inspect which one a repository actually provides.
example: Two requests use the same prompt IDs. The second uses a different adapter that changes attention. Can it reuse the first request’s KV?
The first request’s keys and values were calculated using its base weights and adapter. They are numerical results of that particular computation, rather than copies of the raw prompt IDs.

The second adapter can produce different attention state for the same IDs. Reusing the first state would silently combine values from two different models. Equal shapes do not make the values interchangeable.

Keep compatible model and adapter identity in the cache’s namespace or invalidate the relevant state on a change. Check the behavior by comparing cached results with uncached reference results while alternating the two adapters.

questions.prompt: Paging and prefix caching are…
options: Allocation management versus reuse of computed prefixes
questions.why: They can compose but address different waste. A cache must save the right computation, under a compatible model, and retrieve it cheaply enough to help.
questions.hint: One asks where state fits; the other asks whether it already exists.

questions.prompt: Double batch and context length, holding all else fixed. Raw KV becomes…
questions.why: Both are multiplicative factors in the conventional cache formula.
questions.hint: Multiply the independent scaling factors.

questions.prompt: Same token IDs, different LoRA adapter. Reuse old KV by default?
options: No: adapter identity may change cached computation
Yes, if both adapters have the same rank
questions.why: Equal dimensions do not imply equal hidden states.
questions.hint: What inputs determine the actual keys and values?

transfer: A cache finds more matching prefixes, but requests take longer. Give a possible explanation and a measurement that would test it.
Includes transfer or lookup cost
Compares saved computation with added cost
Measures latency, not hit rate alone

Looking up or fetching the saved state may take longer than processing the prefix again. A cache hit is evidence that stored work was found, not that retrieving it saved time overall. I would separately time lookup, transfer, and remaining prompt computation for hits and misses, then compare time to first token on a representative workload. I would also check whether transfers slow down other requests.
LESSONS.takeaway: A cache must save the right computation, under a compatible model, and retrieve it cheaply enough to help.

LESSONS.title: Compressed attention, sliding windows and replay
LESSONS.goal: Understand what changes when a model compresses, shares, or reconstructs its attention state.
LESSONS.recall: Why is the conventional KV formula not universal?
LESSONS.predict: If each layer sees the last 128 tokens, is the entire multi-layer model’s dependence limited to 128 original tokens?
layers:
A KV cache does not have one universal format.

Our first explanation treated attention state as a collection of keys and values saved for every relevant layer and position. That is a useful starting point, but model designers can change what is represented and how later layers use it.

Those choices matter to engine work. A memory-saving trick that fits one architecture may be invalid for another, even when both models are called transformers.

Compression changes what is stored.

Multi-head latent attention, abbreviated MLA, uses a compressed numerical representation instead of the conventional full cache layout. This is a change to how the model represents attention information. It is different from paging, which organizes where allocated blocks live.

A window changes what a query can directly read.

Sliding-window attention limits a position’s direct attention to a recent region. For example, a layer might allow a query to read only the last 128 positions. This can bound some local attention work and state.

But layers build on one another. A recent position’s representation may already contain information from older positions processed in earlier layers. A 128-position window in each layer does not mean the entire model has forgotten everything earlier than 128 original tokens.

Sharing changes which layers must do separate work.

Some architectures allow later layers to use state produced by earlier layers. YOCO, short for “You Only Cache Once,” is useful historical background for this kind of design. DeepInfer has model-specific producer and consumer layer paths; their meaning comes from the supported model configuration.

Replaying a short segment can be an approximation.

DeepInfer’s deployment explanation describes rebuilding local sliding-window state by replaying a recent 128-token segment with truncated visibility. It explicitly describes an approximate reconstruction. The computation deliberately avoids rebuilding every upstream dependency.

That can be a useful engineering tradeoff. The important question is what changed and how much it affects the task. Showing that two implementations of the same shortcut agree is different from showing that the shortcut equals the full original computation.

When reading this code, keep asking what is stored, what is reused, and what is recomputed. Then choose a numerical and task-level comparison that tests the actual promise being made.

Trace a dependency across two layers. A recent token can read an older token in the first layer. A later token can then read that recent token’s updated representation in the second layer. Information has moved farther than one layer’s direct window.

This is the missing step in the argument that replaying one local window must always reconstruct all deeper state exactly. Exact replay bounds require architectural reasoning about the whole dependency path.

DeepInfer’s YoCo code explicitly separates producer and consumer layers using the model configuration. Its compaction path gathers retained positions and updates shared metadata. This is a model-aware execution path, not a general trick you can turn on for arbitrary weights.

The deployment Q&A describes SWA bounded replay: reconstruct local SWA state from a recent 128-token segment with truncated visibility. It is explicitly approximate. Reusing existing block KV and rebuilding local state are separate actions.

Do not confuse “mask and compact implementations agree” with “bounded replay equals full exact reconstruction.” They are different comparisons.

A metadata check tests things such as retained positions, visible ranges, and storage slots. A numerical check compares the values produced under a shared trajectory. A task evaluation measures whether a difference changes useful behavior. These tests answer different questions; none should be described as proving more than it actually checks.

Approximation requires a declared reference and a quality budget: compare teacher-forced log probabilities and task outcomes on representative contexts, especially window boundaries and long dependencies.

DeepInfer’s supplied equivalence checks distinguish metadata-level checks from weight-backed logprob checks. Read the constraints on the compatible checkpoint before interpreting a pass.

Optimization judgment: identify which state is stored, reconstructed or shared; determine the dependency it relies on; then ask what its oracle proves. Generic cache intuition is not enough to modify this path safely.
example: An engineer says a 128-token attention window proves that replaying 128 raw tokens exactly restores a 20-layer model. What is missing?

Start with the first token in the replayed region. In the original run, its deeper representation may have incorporated information that arrived through earlier layers from before the replay boundary.

If replay starts at that boundary without the missing upstream state, it can calculate a different deeper representation. Keeping the same tensor dimensions does not restore the lost numerical information.

Treat exactness as something to establish separately. Compare the replayed and full reference computations on identical continuations, including boundary and long-context cases. If approximation is acceptable, also evaluate the tasks you intend to serve.

questions.prompt: MLA, paging and SWA primarily concern…
options: They all describe the same memory-allocation technique.
They concern what is stored, how memory is organized, and which positions can be read.
They only change how text is split into tokens.
questions.why: Separate what is stored, where it is stored and what is attended to. A smaller cache can come from a different representation, different visibility, or an approximation. Those are different promises.
questions.hint: Ask a different question for each term.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer bounded SWA replay should be described as…
questions.why: The Q&A names the approximation. Exactness is not supplied by a short window alone.
questions.hint: Look at the replay boundary’s missing context.

questions.prompt: Mask-vs-compact logprobs agree. This proves…
options: Every approximation in the whole service is exact
Those implementations agree under the tested conditions
questions.why: A comparison proves only the stated equivalence over its tested inputs and configuration.
questions.hint: Identify the two things actually compared.

transfer: Why would you avoid turning on a model-specific cache shortcut for an arbitrary model you fine-tuned?
Names architecture/config dependency
Distinguishes exactness from approximation
Requires reference and task-quality comparison

A shortcut can depend on how that architecture produces and consumes state. Another model may not have the same layer-sharing or attention dependencies. I would establish compatibility first, then identify whether the shortcut promises exact calculation or accepts an approximation. I would compare against the appropriate reference, test boundary and long-context cases, and evaluate task quality where numerical differences are allowed.
LESSONS.takeaway: A smaller cache can come from a different representation, different visibility, or an approximation. Those are different promises.

LESSONS.title: MoE, parallelism and the slowest worker
LESSONS.goal: Explain what multiple GPUs share, what they split, and why one busy worker can delay the rest.
LESSONS.recall: What is the difference between total parameters and parameters used by one token?
LESSONS.predict: If half the tokens choose experts on one GPU, do equal expert counts guarantee balanced work?
layers:
“Run it on more GPUs” leaves the main design question unanswered.

To use several devices, you need to decide which device stores which weights and performs which work. Different choices create different communication requirements. Before memorizing their abbreviations, ask what is being divided.

Data parallelism divides independent request or token work. Tensor parallelism divides parts of a numerical operation. Pipeline parallelism gives different layers to different devices. Context parallelism divides sequence work. Each name describes the object being split.

Experts add another kind of division.

A mixture of experts, or MoE, contains several feed-forward networks called experts. For each token, a routing mechanism chooses a small subset of them. Many learned expert weights exist, but one token uses only some of them.

This can reduce the arithmetic used for a token, but the weights still have to be stored. With expert parallelism, different devices own different experts. Tokens must reach the devices that hold their selected experts, and the results must be combined afterward.

Equal storage does not guarantee equal work.

Imagine four devices that each store the same number of experts. If the router repeatedly chooses experts on one device, that device receives much more work. The others can finish early and still have to wait for it.

This is why engine developers measure demand per expert and time per device, rather than checking expert counts alone. The communication links between devices matter as well: a fast connection within a machine may behave very differently from a slower connection between machines.

A redundant copy is not a new learned expert.

One response to a hot expert is to place extra physical copies of its weights where they can share the demand. DeepInfer distinguishes logical experts, which are the learned functions the router selects, from physical placements, which include redundant copies.

More copies use more memory and may require work to redistribute. Larger device groups can also add coordination costs. A good design weighs those costs against saved waiting and better use of the hardware.

When you judge a multi-GPU result, draw the ownership and movement of data first. A device count alone does not explain what the system is doing.

A synchronization point makes a group wait for every required participant. If four devices need 5, 5, 5, and 15 milliseconds, the group cannot pass that point in 7.5 milliseconds merely because 7.5 is the mean. The slowest required participant sets a lower bound of 15 milliseconds.

Load balancing tries to reduce that unevenness. The right measurement concerns actual token demand and runtime, not just the number of objects assigned to each device.

For EP, tokens are routed to expert owners, processed and combined. Communication and small per-expert batches can erase arithmetic savings. Fast within-node links and slower cross-node links are not interchangeable.

In DeepInfer’s expert containers, logical experts selected by the gate are distinct from physical expert copies. Redundant copies can increase placement flexibility without adding new learned functions. Placement, routing and hot-expert replication form a load-balancing problem.

The README lists attention DP/balanced CP and MoE EP/EPLB support. Available features are not identical to the production deployment recipe; inspect the Q&A and configuration for a particular run.

A change that spreads weights over more devices can reduce local weight storage while increasing token movement. A change that replicates hot weights can improve balance while consuming extra memory. Neither has a universal winner. Check the workload, network topology, expert selection patterns, and size of the numerical operations that remain on each device.

If rank work takes [5,5,5,15] ms before a barrier, this part costs at least 15 ms. The mean is 7.5 ms, but mean-based arithmetic hides the tail. Moving work or replicating a hot expert may help, at the cost of memory and redistribution traffic.

A larger EP group can aggregate more token work per expert and spread weight ownership, while increasing synchronization and network demands. There is no unconditional “more GPUs is faster” rule.

When judging a distributed design, sketch model state ownership, token movement, collectives and the actual link topology before reading benchmark charts.
example: Four devices finish their required work in 5, 5, 5, and 15 milliseconds, then synchronize. When can the group continue?
At five milliseconds, three devices are ready. Their local work has finished, but the fourth device is still doing work that the next group operation needs.
The average completion time is 7.5 milliseconds, but an average does not satisfy the dependency. The group cannot continue until the fourth device finishes at fifteen milliseconds.

A useful next investigation is why that device is slower. It might have hotter experts, more tokens, slower communication, or different-sized operations. Moving or replicating the right work could help; adding devices without addressing the cause might not.

questions.prompt: Which scheme puts different experts on different GPUs?
questions.why: Expert parallelism partitions expert ownership. Adding devices helps only when useful work and communication are organized well enough to benefit.
questions.hint: Name the object being split.

questions.prompt: Same number of experts per rank means same execution time.
questions.why: Token demand per expert can be uneven.
questions.hint: Equal capacity is not equal demand.

questions.prompt: Four ranks take 5,5,5,15 ms then synchronize. Phase lower bound?
questions.why: The barrier waits for the slowest required participant.
questions.hint: Who has not finished at 7.5 ms?

transfer: An expert model gets little faster when you double its GPU count. Suggest two possible causes and how you would investigate them.
Includes routing skew or small expert batches
Includes communication/topology
Names a measurement per hypothesis

The router might send disproportionate work to a few experts, so some devices finish early and wait. I would measure token demand and execution time per expert and device. Communication might also cost more as the group grows, especially across slower links. I would measure those transfers and inspect where experts are placed. Equal expert counts and more devices do not establish balanced useful work.
LESSONS.takeaway: Adding devices helps only when useful work and communication are organized well enough to benefit.

LESSONS.title: Speculative decoding and DSpark
LESSONS.goal: Explain how guessing several tokens can save time without letting the guesses replace the target model.
LESSONS.recall: What prevents ordinary autoregressive generation from predicting many unknown steps independently?
LESSONS.predict: If draft length doubles, must accepted tokens per second double?
layers:
Generation has an expensive chain of dependencies.

In ordinary generation, the model chooses one next token before it knows the input for a later prediction. If each round is expensive, waiting for those rounds one after another can limit how quickly one person receives an answer.

Speculative decoding tries to get more useful progress out of a target-model round. A cheaper drafter proposes several tokens. The main model, called the target model, then evaluates those proposed positions together.

A proposal is not yet an answer.

The target model checks the proposed continuation. Some draft tokens are accepted; a rejected position is corrected. The details of that acceptance and correction rule matter. Exact speculative sampling is designed to preserve the target model’s output probability distribution under its assumptions.

That promise does not mean every implementation will produce the same exact string for the same seed. Two draws from the same valid probability distribution can differ. Matching distributions and matching one random execution are different properties.

Later guesses depend on earlier guesses surviving.

Suppose a drafter proposes three tokens. The third proposed token is useful as part of the accepted prefix only if the earlier proposals also survive. You cannot count each position as if it contributes independently.

This makes long drafts a tradeoff. They offer a chance to advance farther, but their later positions can be unlikely to survive. Evaluating those positions still consumes work that might have served another request.

DSpark makes that budget choice more deliberate.

The DSpark work combines a draft design with confidence-based verification scheduling. The system estimates how likely proposed prefixes are to survive, and considers how its hardware performs at different amounts of verification work.

DeepInfer contains a related scheduling path that turns confidence information into per-request work lengths. Our small experiment isolates the intuition behind that choice; it does not reproduce the whole production scheduler.

To evaluate speculation for your model, measure useful tokens accepted per round alongside the time spent drafting and checking them. A high acceptance percentage alone does not prove a speedup, and a setting that helps one user may waste capacity when many users are active.

If the first draft has an 80% chance of surviving and the second has an 80% chance given that the first survived, both survive with probability 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. To count expected accepted drafts, add the probability that the first survives, the first two survive, and so on.

The exact acceptance-and-correction rule is more detailed than checking whether the target’s favorite token matches a guess. The formula below concerns preserving a sampling distribution.

For exact speculative sampling, a draft token drawn from q can be accepted with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)), followed on rejection by sampling from a normalized positive residual max(0,p−q). The full algorithm includes prefix handling and a target token after full acceptance.

Exactness here is an output-distribution promise, not a promise of identical random draws or identical strings for the same seed across implementations. Greedy verification has its own simpler match rule.

DSpark’s paper describes balancing prefix survival estimates against a hardware throughput profile. A late token is useful only if earlier draft tokens survive.

An estimate of accepted length becomes an engineering decision only after you include the cost of verifying that length. Hardware throughput is not necessarily linear in the number of proposed tokens. A practical scheduler uses a measured cost profile and handles the mandatory target work in addition to optional draft positions.

If per-position conditional acceptance probabilities are a₁…aₖ, expected accepted drafts are Σᵢ Πⱼ≤ᵢ aⱼ. This assumes acceptance probabilities under the reached prefix and ignores the target correction/bonus token.

DeepInfer’s confidence kernel computes cumulative products, ranks candidate positions across requests, and assigns query lengths under a total budget. Its code is the place to inspect how confidence becomes scheduled work.

Do not guess that longer drafts or higher acceptance improve goodput. Measure drafting time, verification cost, accepted output per round and inter-token latency at the intended concurrency.
example: Two proposed tokens each have a 50% conditional acceptance rate. How many accepted draft tokens do you expect?
The first token contributes one accepted token in half the cases. Its expected contribution is therefore 0.5 tokens.

The second token contributes only when the first survives and the second then survives too. That probability is 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Adding 0.5 for the second directly would forget the first requirement.

Add the contributions: 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 accepted draft tokens on average. This count excludes a target correction or bonus token. To choose a fast setting, you still need the time spent producing and checking those proposals.

questions.prompt: Why verify a draft with the target model?
options: To preserve the target’s intended generation behavior
To avoid loading target weights forever
questions.why: Drafts are proposals; the target remains the reference. Drafting helps when accepted progress is worth more than the work spent drafting and verifying it.
questions.hint: Who decides what output is acceptable?

questions.prompt: Two draft positions each survive conditionally with p=0.5. Expected accepted drafts?
questions.why: 0.5 + 0.5×0.5 = 0.75. The second counts only when the first survives.
questions.hint: Accepted prefixes must be contiguous.

questions.prompt: An exact speculative sampler promises…
options: Identical strings for all hardware and seeds
The target output distribution, assuming the algorithm’s conditions
questions.why: Distributional equality differs from pathwise equality.
questions.hint: Think about two valid random samples from the same distribution.

transfer: Explain how longer drafts could help one user receive tokens faster but reduce the amount of useful work the server does for everyone.
Names saved serial rounds
Names added low-value verification work
Includes concurrency or capacity constraint

A single user may advance through several accepted tokens in one target-model round, reducing serial waits. But later draft positions have to survive all earlier positions, so some extra checking has little chance of helping. With many requests active, that verification consumes capacity that could serve other users. I would measure accepted progress, drafting and checking time, and latency at the intended concurrency rather than choosing the longest draft by default.
LESSONS.takeaway: Drafting helps when accepted progress is worth more than the work spent drafting and verifying it.

LESSONS.title: Correctness, determinism and structured output
LESSONS.goal: Choose a check that tests the specific kind of correctness your change promises.
LESSONS.recall: How does equal output distribution differ from identical outputs?
LESSONS.predict: If JSON parses successfully, have you proved the answer’s facts are true?
layers:
