A believable answer can still come from a broken engine.

Suppose you change how a model reads its cache. The program runs, the response sounds fluent, and its JSON parses. Have you shown that the change preserved the model’s calculation? Each observation is useful, but none directly answers that question.

An array can have the right dimensions and contain the wrong numbers. A paragraph can sound sensible while differing from the reference model. A JSON object can be structurally valid and contain false facts.

JSON is a structured text format that programs can parse into fields and values. A grammar can restrict which continuations are allowed so an answer follows that format. This helps with structure, but a correctly formatted field can still contain the wrong date or an invented fact.

Start by naming the property you want to preserve.

For an exact attention implementation, you may want numerical outputs to match a reference within a stated rounding tolerance. For an exact sampling method, you may be preserving a probability distribution. For a deliberate approximation, you may accept numerical differences only if task quality stays within an agreed limit.

A reference is a trusted comparison path, often a simpler implementation. People sometimes call a check like this an oracle: something that tells you whether the property being tested holds. The name does not make the reference infallible; you still need to understand what it checks.

Control the input when you compare outputs.

If two generators choose different tokens, their later inputs also differ. Later output differences then become hard to interpret. You can instead feed both implementations the same known continuation and compare their predictions at the same positions. This is called teacher forcing.

That comparison helps locate the first disagreement before different generated histories hide its cause.

Test the cases a pleasant example can miss.

A cache bug might appear only when a sequence crosses a block boundary. A state leak might require two requests to run in an interleaved order. A sampling bug might appear when a stop token is proposed inside a draft. Design the case that exercises the property instead of relying only on an ordinary chat.

Deterministic sampling and batch invariance are also separate promises. A seed controls random draws; batch invariance concerns whether a request changes when its batch companions change. You need more than a seed to assume every numerical execution behaves identically.

Your job is to say exactly what your evidence establishes, then leave the other questions visible.

Use checks at several boundaries. Validate shapes and indexes to catch structural mistakes. Compare intermediate values and logits to test the calculation. Check generated tokens under controlled settings to test the generation loop. Finally, evaluate the tasks you care about to see whether model behavior is useful.

These checks complement one another. Passing a lower-level check does not automatically establish all the higher-level properties.

Useful checks form a ladder: shape and index invariants; reference-vs-optimized logits on shared prefixes; greedy token equality; sampling-distribution checks; task-level evaluation. Passing a lower rung does not imply the higher ones.

For grammar constraints, the automaton state tracks allowed continuations. A token mask changes the sampler’s legal set. Chunk boundaries, tokenization and stop behavior all matter.

DeepInfer’s sampler contains verification logic and structured-output masking. Its offline example enables batch-invariant behavior on its NVIDIA path; read supported platform/configuration scope before generalizing.

A tolerance is a declared allowance for numerical difference, not a way to ignore unexplained mismatches. Choose one appropriate to the operation and numerical format, and investigate patterns such as sudden errors at a cache boundary. An approximation deserves its own explicitly different quality contract rather than quietly weakening the promise of an exact rewrite.

Exercise adversarial boundaries: cache reset, zero/one-token lengths where valid, maximum context, EOS inside drafts, mixed request lengths, different co-batches and adapter switches. An incorrect fast path may appear correct on pleasant prompts.

For your own engine, preserve an intentionally simple reference and compare layer outputs when a mismatch appears. Final prose comparison is too weak for debugging attention or positional errors.

Quantization and approximate attention need task-level acceptance criteria. Exact-operation refactors should not silently broaden their contract into “looks about right.”
example: A cache change produces valid JSON, but its numerical predictions disagree with the reference at a page boundary. Would you accept an exactness claim?
The JSON result tells you the output followed a structural constraint. It does not establish that attention read the correct positions or used the correct cached values.

The disagreement on identical prefixes is directly relevant to the claimed numerical equivalence. Look for the first differing position and layer, especially around the boundary where the error appears.

Investigate and repair that mismatch before accepting the exactness claim. If you instead want to allow approximation, state that different contract and test its effect on real task quality; do not infer it from valid formatting.

questions.prompt: A JSON grammar proves…
options: Conformance to the supported structural constraints
questions.why: Structure is a different property from semantic truth. A test can pass while the important property remains untested. Match the check to the claim.
questions.hint: A perfectly formatted wrong answer is still possible.

questions.prompt: A seed by itself guarantees batch invariance.
options: No, numerical execution and RNG assignment also matter
questions.why: Different batching can alter reductions or draw assignment unless controlled.
questions.hint: What happens before random selection?

questions.prompt: Best first oracle for an exact attention-kernel rewrite?
options: Matching layer outputs against a reference over varied shapes
A user says responses feel good
questions.why: Test the numerical claim at the operator boundary before measuring downstream behavior.
questions.hint: Pin the promised invariant directly.

transfer: Pick an engine change and describe what you would compare to decide whether it is correct. Say what the comparison would and would not establish.
Names a reference
States equality/tolerance/quality criterion
States tested configurations and boundaries

For a cache-read change, I would feed identical token prefixes to the full reference calculation and the cached path, then compare the next-token scores within a stated tolerance. I would include cache boundaries and interleaved requests. That directly tests the numerical property under those conditions. It does not prove every possible configuration or that the model gives factually correct answers, so other claims need their own checks.
LESSONS.takeaway: A test can pass while the important property remains untested. Match the check to the claim.

activity.title: Check the numbers before judging a fluent answer.
activity.intro: Two paths receive the same fixed input IDs [1, 4]. The reference returns next-token scores [0.2, 0.8, -0.1]. A changed path returns [0.2, 0.805, -0.1]. Your stated rule permits an absolute difference of at most 0.001 in every score. Both paths still choose the second token when selecting the highest score.

fields.label: What is the largest absolute score difference?
fields.why: The second entry differs by 0.805 − 0.8 = 0.005. The other entries match.

fields.label: Does the changed path pass the stated numerical rule?
options: Yes, because it chooses the same token
No, because one score difference exceeds the tolerance
fields.why: 0.005 is greater than 0.001. Matching the highest-scoring token does not establish that the numerical comparison passed.

activity.conclusion: A useful correctness check needs fixed inputs, a reference, a comparison rule, and a boundary. Passing this one numerical case would still leave request isolation, stop behavior, and task quality to check.

LESSONS.title: From a fast engine to a usable service
LESSONS.goal: Trace the work around a model calculation and understand when separating stages is worth it.
LESSONS.recall: Which parts of an online service live outside an engine loop?
LESSONS.predict: Can separating prefill and decode make things slower for a small workload?
layers:
The GPU calculation is only part of a request’s journey.

A user sends a question, but a machine must receive it, check access, prepare its text, choose a worker, and perhaps wait for space. After the model runs, the response must be converted back to text and delivered. Any part of that path can add delay or fail.

This surrounding system is what turns an engine into a service. Keeping that distinction clear helps you understand both a production architecture diagram and the limits of an open-source engine release.

Some systems put different stages on different workers.

Prefill processes the known prompt; decode extends the answer. Because their workloads differ, a large deployment can give each stage its own resources and scheduling. Separating stages like this is called disaggregation.

A multimodal system may also separate the work that turns images into model representations. That does not make the stages independent: later stages need the numerical state produced by earlier ones.

A separation creates a handoff.

If one machine processes the prompt and another continues the answer, the necessary state must move between them. That takes bandwidth, adds a dependency, and creates another place where a failure needs handling.

Independent scaling can make those costs worthwhile for a large or uneven workload. A small workload may be better served by a simpler arrangement that keeps the stages together. You need measurements to decide.

A queue does not create more capacity.

When requests arrive faster than they can finish, unfinished work accumulates. Letting the queue grow without limit can make some users wait an extremely long time. A service needs a policy: how much work to admit, how long to wait, and what to do when those limits are reached.

It also needs to release resources when a user cancels or a request times out. Otherwise finished or abandoned work can keep consuming memory and scheduler slots.

Begin with a system you can explain.

For your first fine-tuned-model service, start with one compatible engine and a representative workload. Establish that it loads the intended model and produces the expected behavior. Then measure which part of the journey needs improvement before reproducing a much larger production architecture.

Draw the full request path and label each place that owns state. A queue owns pending requests. A running engine owns working attention state. A transfer protocol must define when another worker can take over. Streaming must preserve the order and ownership of output.

A boundary is useful only when you understand both what crosses it and what happens if that crossing fails.

Draw the path: request → format/tokenize → queue → prefill → transfer state → decode → detokenize/stream. Add prefix lookup, admission control and cancellation. Every arrow can add latency or fail.

The DeepSeek Q&A describes a larger E/P/D system and separate cache storage. The open-source README explicitly bounds what is included. Production architecture diagrams must not be mistaken for a runnable public deployment bundle.

Independent scaling can help when prompt work and output work vary differently. State transfer must fit the network budget and reliability requirements.

A distributed design is partly a failure-handling design. If a worker disappears, decide whether a request fails, retries, or resumes elsewhere. Resuming requires compatible complete state and a clear owner of future output. These are correctness responsibilities in addition to performance decisions.

Design overload behavior deliberately: reject, queue with a deadline, or reduce admitted work within an explicit product contract. Unbounded queues transform a capacity problem into extreme tail latency.

Cancellation must release cache and scheduler slots. Migration needs complete state and a single owner of further output. Cache isolation must include model/adapters and access boundaries where applicable.

For your first tuned-model service, begin with one compatible engine and a fixed representative workload. Establish observability and correctness before distributed architecture experiments.
example: Fetching a remote prefix cache takes 18 milliseconds but saves 10 milliseconds of prefill. Does the cache hit help?
First compare the work saved with the work added. Under a simple no-overlap assumption, saving ten milliseconds while adding eighteen makes the request eight milliseconds slower.

Now ask whether fetching can overlap other useful work. Also check whether the transfer competes for bandwidth with other requests. Those details could change the result, so measure the relevant stages separately.
Report the user-visible latency result alongside hit rate. Finding more cached prefixes is only beneficial if the overall system uses that stored work effectively.

questions.prompt: Disaggregation introduces a need to…
questions.why: The next stage needs the computed context/state. A fast engine needs queues, routing, state transfer, and failure handling around it to become a usable service.
questions.hint: What did prefill produce that decode consumes?

questions.prompt: Which is a good first deployment goal?
options: Reproduce a huge production cluster immediately
A correct compatible single-engine baseline with measurements
questions.why: A reference baseline makes later complexity measurable.
questions.hint: Start where failure causes are easiest to isolate.

questions.prompt: Under overload, an unbounded queue primarily risks…
questions.why: Excess work waits longer and consumes resources without adding capacity.
questions.hint: Arrival rate can exceed completion rate.

transfer: Describe a simple service for your fine-tuned model. Where does unfinished work live, and what should happen when a user cancels?
Identifies request queue and KV ownership
Includes model/tokenizer/adapter identity
Names cancellation/timeout handling

Requests first wait in a bounded queue and then run in a compatible engine. Each active request owns its model working state, including its attention cache. The service must know which base, adapter, and input format are in use. Completion or cancellation should release the request’s slots and state when no consumer still needs them. I would establish this simple path before adding remote transfers or separately scaled stages.
LESSONS.takeaway: A fast engine needs queues, routing, state transfer, and failure handling around it to become a usable service.

LESSONS.title: Read DeepInfer without getting lost
LESSONS.goal: Follow one request through DeepInfer before exploring individual optimizations.
LESSONS.recall: What evidence separates an engine feature from a production service feature?
LESSONS.predict: Will reading every kernel before the request loop give you the best first map?
layers:
You do not need to understand every file before you can understand one path.

Opening a large engine repository can feel like being dropped into the middle of a conversation. There are kernels, worker processes, configuration options, and several ways to represent a request. Reading files alphabetically rarely explains how those pieces cooperate.

Instead, choose one concrete question: “What happens when this example asks the model to generate a response?” Follow that request from input to output. Each function you encounter should answer a smaller part of the question.

Begin with the example’s inputs.

Open examples/offline_inference.py. Find where it chooses a model, configures how many devices participate, creates the engine, and asks for outputs. You do not need to understand every option yet. Write down what the example passes into generation and what it expects back.

Find the public entry point.

Next open deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py. The generation method admits requests and runs a loop until they finish. Follow the call that adds a request, then the loop that collects its outputs.

Ask where the request’s identity comes from, which state belongs to it, and how its results are put back in order. Those questions connect the code to the engine responsibilities you already understand.

Then follow one execution step.

In deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py, locate the step method, scheduling, asynchronous execution, and result handling. The scheduler chooses work; the model execution performs it; post-processing updates request state. Trace that sequence before diving into its kernels.

Choose one detail worth investigating.

For example, the entry point clones output objects before the next step can reuse their underlying storage. That is a reason to investigate data lifetime, not automatically a copy to delete for speed.

Or follow sampling into sampler.py to distinguish ordinary token selection from draft verification. Pick one responsibility and find the inputs and outputs it owns.

Keep your notes honest: distinguish what you directly observed in code from what the authors report and what you infer. The source links here pin a particular revision so someone else can open the same code you read.

For each call, write one sentence: “This function receives ___, decides or calculates ___, and returns or changes ___.” If a sentence contains something you cannot explain, follow that one dependency. This keeps the reading task bounded and reveals where a useful test could attach.

A vertical path is a map for later exploration. It is not evidence that you have inspected every possible configuration or execution path.

  1. examples/offline_inference.py: find EP/DP/CP arguments and model creation.
  2. deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py: follow generate → _add_request → _run_engine. Notice result ordering and output cloning.
  3. deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py: find step → schedule → async execution → post_process.
  4. deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sampler.py: distinguish logits, grammar masking and verification.
  5. schedule_mtp_varlen.py: find cumulative confidence, top-budget selection and query lengths.

Do not begin by changing flags. First predict which function should run and prove it using a trace or a tiny test.

A focused first engine change can be a missing boundary test, a loader fix, or a correction to an inaccurate benchmark. Begin with a reproducible observation and an invariant you can check. The size of a kernel rewrite is not a measure of whether the contribution is valuable.

Choose one seam: confidence scheduling. Identify inputs, valid ranges, the mandatory target-token budget, tie-breaking and prefix closure. Then construct a small reference computation and compare it to the implementation.

The browser lab simplifies selection to expected accepted drafts under a fixed budget. The real engine includes target slots, hardware profiles and asynchronous metadata. Treat the lab as conceptual scaffolding, not a drop-in replacement.

A credible first contribution can be a bounded boundary test, a reproducible benchmark correction or a focused lifetime fix. A novel kernel is not the only meaningful engine work.
example: You find an output clone inside the generation loop. How do you decide whether it is unnecessary?

Find out what raw output points to. In this entry point, the nearby code and comment concern storage that a later engine step can release or reuse. A list append alone would retain a reference rather than guarantee a stable independent value.
Trace when the consumer reads the stored result and when the producer can overwrite the underlying buffer. The copy may be the operation that keeps those lifetimes from conflicting.

Before removing it, construct a test that saves one output, forces later buffer reuse, and then reads the earlier output. Any replacement must preserve the earlier value through copying or a proven ownership protocol.

questions.prompt: Best first reading route?
options: Start with an example and follow one request through to its results.
Read every file in alphabetical order before following any requests.
Read the benchmark charts without checking the execution path.
questions.why: A vertical slice builds a map tied to observable behavior. Build a map by following one request, then investigate one responsibility at a time.
questions.hint: Follow one request, not the directory tree.

questions.prompt: A code link should pin a commit because…
options: It identifies the revision supporting the explanation
questions.why: Readers can reproduce the source context rather than opening changed main.
questions.hint: What will a future reader actually see?

questions.prompt: An output clone before reusing buffers is likely worth checking for…
questions.why: Removing a copy can change whether a consumer reads valid data.
questions.hint: Relate the copy to async reuse.

transfer: Trace one request through DeepInfer in a few sentences. Name one property you would test at a specific boundary.
Traces entrypoint to scheduling to execution to sampling
Names request-owned state
Names an observable invariant

The example creates the model and calls generation. The entry point admits requests, then repeatedly asks the engine to schedule and execute work. Model execution produces values used by sampling, and result handling updates the requests and collects their outputs. Each request needs its own state. At the output-collection boundary, I would test that an earlier saved output remains unchanged after a later step reuses the producer’s buffer.
LESSONS.takeaway: Build a map by following one request, then investigate one responsibility at a time.

activity.title: Trace one request and name the promise at one boundary.
activity.intro: Open the pinned entrypoint below. Start with generate, follow the loop that collects outputs, and find where an output is copied before it is kept. You are reading a small path, not auditing the whole engine.

fields.label: In your own words, what enters and leaves this path?
fields.placeholder: The caller provides… The engine repeatedly… The caller eventually receives…

fields.label: Choose one boundary and state what must stay true.
fields.placeholder: At the point where an output is saved, it must…

fields.label: What small test would expose a violation?
fields.placeholder: Produce one result, then… Read it again and compare…

compare: Follow the actual function calls and saved values. A function name alone does not explain its responsibility.
One useful promise is that a result kept for the caller stays unchanged after the engine reuses temporary storage.
Use distinguishable outputs and read the first saved value after a later engine step. Shapes alone would not expose a changed value.
activity.example: For the output-copy boundary, I would create an output containing token 7, let the collector save it, then reuse the producer’s storage for token 9. The saved first output should still contain 7. This checks one lifetime promise, rather than proving every engine path correct.

LESSONS.title: Your fine-tuned model is more than a weights file
LESSONS.goal: Know which files and settings you need to reproduce the model you fine-tuned.
LESSONS.recall: Why can the wrong tokenizer make correct weights behave incorrectly?
LESSONS.predict: If two checkpoints share an architecture name, can you apply the same LoRA adapter to either base revision?
layers:
A file full of learned numbers is not the whole agreement.

Suppose you fine-tune a base model and want to run the result in an inference engine. It is tempting to think the job is finished once you have a weights file. But the computer also needs to know what those numbers mean and how inputs were represented during training.

An engine must support the model’s architecture: the arrangement of layers and calculations described by its configuration. Fine-tuning a model does not automatically turn that architecture into a different one that another engine knows how to execute.

An adapter may contain only the change.

With LoRA, a common fine-tuning method, you train a compact update attached to selected base-model matrices. The saved adapter typically does not include all the original base weights. Running it requires the compatible base as well as the adapter’s configuration and learned values.

Two base revisions can have exactly the same dimensions and still contain different learned numbers. An adapter trained against one is not proved correct against the other merely because it loads without a shape error.

Text formatting is part of what the model learned.

A tokenizer assigns IDs to text pieces and special markers. A chat template arranges messages and roles into the token sequence a chat-trained model expects. A completion model may instead expect the custom format you used in training.

Changing these inputs can change behavior even while every learned weight loads successfully. Keep the intended tokenizer, input format, and stop-token behavior with the model.

Record enough information to rebuild the same computation.

A small artifact manifest is a record of the pieces you used: the exact base revision, adapter or merged weights, model configuration, tokenizer and format, numerical precision, and relevant library versions. “Latest base” is not a stable identity.

You can either serve an adapter alongside its supported base or merge its learned update into compatible full weights where the tooling allows it. Those paths need their own checks, particularly when reduced precision or quantization is involved.

Before optimizing, load the intended combination in a reference path and save a few fixed inputs with expected numerical or task-level behavior. That gives you something concrete to compare when an engine appears to run the model successfully.

LoRA represents a large update through two smaller matrices. Applying the update during execution and multiplying it out into a merged weight matrix are algebraically equivalent in real-number arithmetic. The equation below expresses those two routes.

Actual computers round intermediate results, so changing the order of operations can introduce small differences. Evaluate those differences under a stated numerical tolerance and task check.

For a weight W, ordinary LoRA uses W′=W+sBA, where A and B have small inner rank and s is a scaling factor. For row-vector input, compare x(W+sBA)ᵀ with xWᵀ+s(xAᵀ)Bᵀ.

Two deployment choices: serve a supported adapter alongside its exact base, or merge the update into a compatible floating-point model and save a complete checkpoint. Verify what your framework/version supports; quantized or variant adapters may have additional restrictions.

Merging can change rounding. Equal algebra in real numbers is not a demand for bitwise equality in every numeric format.

The model identity that matters for loading also matters for caching. An adapter can change intermediate attention state. If you switch adapters while reusing incompatible state from an earlier request, you can calculate a hybrid result that corresponds to neither intended model. Test adapter changes as well as initial loading.

Create an artifact manifest: base ID and immutable revision; architecture/config hash; tokenizer/template identity; adapter target modules, rank and scaling; precision/quantization method; library versions; context settings; evaluation dataset revision. Avoid mutable names as your only provenance.

Use a fixed holdout set with known desired behavior to compare base, adapted reference and engine output. Check token IDs before logits. For a base model trained as a completion model, do not invent a chat template unless your fine-tuning established one.

Adapter identity belongs in cache compatibility. Switching adapters without invalidating relevant state can silently run a hybrid computation.
example: An adapter trained on base revision R1 loads on R2 without a shape error. Have you established that it is the model you trained?

LESSONS.title: What a cache must remember
LESSONS.goal: Read one cache slice, predict what it removes, and repair it using actual model scores.
LESSONS.recall: What exact numerical comparison establishes cache correctness?
LESSONS.predict: If a cache accidentally drops its first key/value, will matching tensor shapes detect it?
layers:
This lesson teaches one thing: a cache can avoid repeating earlier calculations, but attention must still read the history it needs. You will trace two token positions, then repair a one-line change that silently removes part of that history.

Read the slice before running the model.

Python counts positions from zero. With two saved entries, [0:] selects positions 0 and 1. [1:] selects only position 1. The colon means “from here to the end.” The original arrays stay the same size; the slice controls which entries the calculation receives.

What is actually stored?

Each saved entry contains a key and a value: numerical vectors calculated from a token and its position. The query, named q in the code, comes from the current token. Attention compares that query with the visible keys, then uses the resulting weights to mix the corresponding values.

If you remove a saved entry from the read, you remove its possible contribution to that mixture. The rest of the model then calculates its next-token scores from a different mixture. Two arrays can still have equal lengths while representing the wrong calculation.

Here is the question you will answer.

When the second input arrives, why does starting at position 1 change the scores? In “See an example,” watch the actual entries and attention weights at each position. In “Try it,” change the highlighted value, predict which entries remain, and run your version. Finish by explaining why your repair is justified.

The small model uses random weights and numbered tokens. Its purpose here is to make the calculation visible, rather than produce fluent language.

The important property is that two implementations receive the same sequence and calculate the same next-token scores within the chosen tolerance. Generated text is a less precise debugging signal because one changed token changes all later inputs.

For a scheduler, compare each request against its own independent generation. Include requests that finish early and a new request that takes over a freed slot.

Use the code viewer in this lesson to inspect attention, full_logits and cached_step. Predict each tensor’s shape, then trace one prompt token by token. The reference recomputes the full prefix; the cached path retains K/V.

The broken-read experiment in “Try it” activates a deliberately wrong cache boundary. Predict the first divergent prefix, run it, then locate the one-line cause. The result table should show the detected mismatch.

The tests also compare interleaved request states and explicit versus merged low-rank output-head updates. Those updates are constructed examples, not trained adapters or PEFT checkpoint support.

Vectorizing the arithmetic changes how work is executed. Paging the cache changes how state is stored and addressed. Chunking prefill changes how known inputs are divided into work units. Keep those experiments separate at first, so a failure points to a specific new mechanism rather than several simultaneous changes.

  1. Add an explicit maximum-context policy. Define whether you reject or truncate; silently changing attention is not a neutral implementation detail.
  2. Add a scheduler that admits a waiting request after another finishes. Keep separate caches; compare every request with independent generation.
  3. Port matrix operations to NumPy or PyTorch and preserve the reference oracle.
  4. Only then try chunked prefill or paged storage, with tests at page boundaries.

For each extension, compare results with the independent reference. Include early finishes, a new request taking over a freed slot, and cases on both sides of a storage boundary. A scheduler that organizes requests is not yet a fused batched matrix operation; measure the work the implementation actually performs.
example: We process input IDs [1, 4]. These numbers name tokens; they are not the saved attention values.
The first input creates the entry at position 0. With only one entry, attention gives it all of the weight. The cached path and the full-prefix reference use the same information.

The second input creates an additional entry at position 1. Starting the read at 0 keeps both entries. Attention distributes its weight between the two saved values, and the cached scores still agree with the reference.

Now change only the read boundary to 1. Position 0 is still stored, but attention no longer receives it. The remaining entry gets all of the weight. Inspect one next-token score to see the numerical consequence of that missing contribution.

questions.why: The slice begins at index 1 and continues to the end. It leaves position 0 out of the values passed to attention, even though that entry still exists in the cache.
questions.hint: Python starts counting at zero. The number before the colon is the first included position.

transfer: Your teammate says: “The keys and values still have equal lengths, so starting the cache read at 1 is safe.” Explain what the code actually omits, how that changes the calculation, and what comparison supports your repair.
Names the omitted cache position and its contribution
Connects the changed visible values to changed model scores
Repairs the read boundary and compares with the same full-prefix reference

With two saved positions, starting at 1 omits position 0 from both slices. Equal slice lengths only show that keys and values are paired; they do not show that the intended history is present. Attention mixes only the remaining value, so later model calculations can produce different next-token scores. Starting at 0 restores both positions. I would compare cached and full-prefix scores on the same inputs, including the second position where this bug first appears. Matching those checks supports this repair; it does not establish a speedup.
LESSONS.takeaway: A cache must preserve the right history, not merely two arrays with matching lengths.

LESSONS.title: Serve your first real fine-tuned model
LESSONS.goal: Move your fine-tuned model into a compatible engine and check that it still behaves as intended.
LESSONS.recall: What must match between training-time prompt formatting and inference?
LESSONS.predict: If the server returns HTTP 200, do you know it is using your adapter?
layers:
Make the first deployment a controlled comparison.

You now have two related goals: run the model you actually trained, and run it efficiently. Establish the first before using the second to justify changes. Otherwise, an output difference can be hard to attribute to the model files, input format, numerical format, or engine.

Choose an engine by the calculations it supports.

Start with the exact architecture and configuration of your base model. Check whether the engine supports that architecture, the adapter path you use, and the numerical format you plan to serve.

DeepInfer is our advanced case study. Its model-specific design is not a promise that it can execute any model fine-tuned from any base. A compatible general-purpose engine may be a more practical first deployment target for your own model.

Save a small set of fixed inputs.

Use the correct tokenizer and training-time format to produce prompt IDs. Record the stop behavior and generation settings. Keep these inputs fixed when comparing the reference and engine.

This prevents a common confusion: two systems receive the same visible question but actually run different token sequences because their formatting differs.

Check the model before putting an API around it.

Load the intended base plus adapter, or the intended merged checkpoint, in the direct reference path. Save numerical predictions where practical and evaluate examples from a held-out task set. A held-out set contains cases you did not use to fit the model, helping you assess behavior beyond the training examples.

Then run the compatible engine on the same inputs. Compare next-token probabilities where available, controlled greedy outputs, and the task results you care about. Be clear when the available comparison is weaker than a direct numerical check.

Add complexity one change at a time.

Once offline generation is correct, add a local endpoint and concurrent requests. Test limits, cancellation, different input lengths, and reloading. Evaluate quantization separately so a quality difference has an identifiable cause.

An HTTP success response tells you that an endpoint answered. It does not, by itself, show that the intended adapter was active or that the model’s behavior was preserved. Keep the artifact identity and reference comparisons alongside the service measurements.

A useful comparison has separate rows for the base reference, the adapted reference, and the adapted model in the engine. An optional fourth row tests quantization. This makes it easier to see whether a difference came from learning, execution, or numerical representation.

Record both task behavior and resource use. A faster configuration is useful only under the quality and latency requirements you actually intend to meet.

  1. Freeze inputs: save prompt IDs, expected stop behavior and generation settings.
  2. Load reference: exact base plus adapter or merged checkpoint; evaluation mode and no gradients.
  3. Compare: teacher-forced logprobs if exposed; otherwise controlled greedy continuations plus task checks, acknowledging the weaker oracle.
  4. Serve: use the engine’s documented offline/API entrypoint and confirm the requested adapter/model identity.
  5. Stress: mixed lengths, cancellation, limits, concurrent requests and a restart/reload.

The activity in this lesson links official support documentation and helps you record the comparison you plan to run. Commands and installation depend on your chosen architecture, accelerator and engine version; do not infer them from DeepInfer examples.

A focused first optimization starts with a trace: which stage consumes time, which resource constrains it, and under what request pattern? Change that one part, preserve the reference checks, and repeat the same workload. This is the bridge between understanding inference vocabulary and doing useful engine work.

Build a controlled comparison table: reference base, reference adapted, engine adapted, optionally engine quantized. Record token agreement, holdout task score, weights/KV memory, TTFT/ITL and throughput. Evaluate quantization as a separate change.

A credible engine contribution for this model is one focused patch backed by a failing oracle, a passing fix and a representative benchmark. A config change, loader support or scheduling correction can qualify if it changes real behavior.

Before paying for hardware, calculate weight plus KV capacity with headroom for activations/workspace. For actual commands, bring your architecture/config and artifact manifest into the tutor; hardware is not assumed by this prototype.
example: The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and says your adapter’s name. What further evidence would show that it runs your adapted model?
Confirm the actual base and adapter artifact identities used by the engine. A response label alone can describe the intended configuration without proving which learned values were loaded.

Compare fixed inputs against the adapted reference. Include a held-out task where the adapted model behaves meaningfully differently from the base, and compare numerical predictions where the engine exposes them.
After establishing that behavior, test concurrent requests, limits, and restart/reload behavior. These service checks complement the model comparison; they do not replace it.

LESSONS.title: Judge a performance claim and test one change
LESSONS.goal: Explain whether an engine change helped, using evidence another person can reproduce.
LESSONS.recall: Which correctness promise did your last optimization actually make?
LESSONS.predict: A chart says 2× faster. What information would let you decide whether that helps your workload?
layers:
A faster-looking chart is the beginning of a question.

Imagine a benchmark claiming twice as many tokens per second. You might want the same improvement for your fine-tuned model. Before deciding, ask what was compared and which conditions made that result possible.

A change in GPU count, numerical format, request length, batch size, or cache state can change the number. If several conditions changed together, the result does not isolate which change caused the gain.

Describe the workload as well as the model.

Record how long the prompts and outputs are, how requests arrive, how many run at once, and whether prefixes are already cached. These conditions determine the kind of work the engine performs.

A configuration that does well on many short requests can behave differently on a small number of long-context requests. “The same model” does not make those workloads equivalent.

Keep quality and latency requirements in the comparison.

If users need a smooth answer, total throughput alone is insufficient. Measure the initial wait, later token gaps, and the slow tail of requests. State which observed percentile must meet your target.

Also keep the correctness promise visible. A numerical approximation that changes task quality is a different tradeoff from an exact rewrite that removes redundant work. Report those differences rather than hiding them in a headline speedup.

Make the result reproducible.

Save the exact model and adapter identities, code revision, hardware, library versions, precision settings, workload, warmup procedure, and measurement commands. Another engineer should be able to tell what ran and what the reported numbers include.

Do not change the workload after seeing a disappointing result without labeling it as a different experiment. Learning that an optimization helps one case and hurts another is useful engineering information.

Apply the comparison in this lesson.

Use the notes and checks you have built during the lessons to choose one justified code or configuration change for a supported deployment of your fine-tuned model. Show the reference comparison, the bottleneck evidence, the modification, and the repeated benchmark. Explain both the gain and its limits.

That is stronger evidence of working understanding than memorizing framework names. It gives you a method you can apply when the next model or engine behaves differently.

Use a matched comparison when you want to isolate one cause: keep artifacts, hardware, inputs, arrival patterns, precision, and cache policy fixed, then change the mechanism under investigation. If perfect matching is impossible, say which differences remain and what narrower conclusion the data supports.

Cost efficiency needs actual cost information and comparable useful work. Counting devices alone is not a complete cost measurement.

Record immutable model/adapter and code revisions; hardware and topology; versions; numeric formats; context and output distributions; arrival process; warmup; cache policy; sample count; failures; p50/p95/p99 TTFT and ITL; useful throughput; memory peaks; task score and tolerances.

Compare at a matched latency/quality requirement. Report both gains and regressions. If the authors report a production improvement, preserve its baseline and operating point rather than turning it into a universal speedup.

Useful experiment sequence: establish correctness → collect a trace → name the bottleneck → change one thing → recheck correctness → rerun the same workload.

A negative result can improve your design judgment. If a longer draft helps one user but reduces useful throughput at your target concurrency, record that tradeoff and the workload where it appears.

Use the work saved inside the lessons to make one comparison reproducible: identify the intended model files, keep a reference, state the workload and quality rule, collect evidence of a limiting resource, then change one mechanism. Keep commands, numerical or task comparisons, measurements, and remaining questions together.

Choose one DeepInfer mechanism—overlap, expert replication, speculative budget, or bounded replay. Explain the resource it might save, the dependency it relies on, and the evidence you would need before using it for your model. A result on one workload should not become a universal recommendation.
example: Configuration A produces 2,000 tokens/s with p99 token gaps of 180 ms. B produces 1,600 tokens/s with p99 gaps of 60 ms. Your limit is 80 ms. Which qualifies?
Apply the requirement before maximizing the attractive number. A’s p99 gap of 180 milliseconds exceeds the stated 80-millisecond limit. B’s 60-millisecond result is within it.

Among these two measured configurations, B qualifies for that latency requirement even though its aggregate throughput is lower. This conclusion assumes their quality checks and measurement boundaries are comparable.

To compare cost efficiency or generalize to another workload, you need more information. Record hardware cost, workload details, and the other relevant measurements rather than treating this small table as a universal ranking.

GLOSSARY.Activation: An intermediate numerical value produced while executing the model.
GLOSSARY.Adapter: A learned modification attached to compatible base weights; LoRA is one family.
GLOSSARY.Autoregressive: Each next-token prediction conditions on earlier tokens.
GLOSSARY.Bandwidth: How many bytes can move per second; distinct from memory capacity.
GLOSSARY.Batch invariance: A supported guarantee that changing co-batch membership does not change a request’s result.
GLOSSARY.BF16 / FP16: Two-byte floating-point formats with different precision/range tradeoffs.
GLOSSARY.Checkpoint: Saved model parameters/configuration at a particular point; may be full weights or only an adapter.
GLOSSARY.Collective: A coordinated communication operation among device ranks, such as all-reduce.
GLOSSARY.CP: Context parallelism: divide sequence work among devices.
GLOSSARY.CUDA graph: A captured device-work graph reused to reduce launch overhead, under shape and memory constraints.
GLOSSARY.Decode: Iteratively extend a sequence using retained model state.
GLOSSARY.DP: Data parallelism: split independent work, with details depending on the layer/system.
GLOSSARY.EPLB: Expert-parallel load balancing: place/map expert work to reduce skew.
GLOSSARY.EP: Expert parallelism: distribute expert ownership across devices.
GLOSSARY.EOS: End-of-sequence marker or corresponding termination condition.
GLOSSARY.FLOP: One floating-point arithmetic operation; FLOP/s measures a rate.
GLOSSARY.GEMM: General matrix multiplication, a central building block of model execution.
GLOSSARY.GQA: Grouped-query attention: query heads share fewer KV heads.
GLOSSARY.HBM: High-bandwidth accelerator memory; capacity and transfer bandwidth are separate limits.
GLOSSARY.Kernel: A device program implementing one or more numerical operations.
GLOSSARY.KV cache: Retained keys and values or compatible attention state for preceding tokens.
GLOSSARY.LoRA: Low-rank adaptation: a compact parameter update to selected base-model matrices.
GLOSSARY.MLA: Multi-head latent attention: compressed attention representations; not a paging scheme.
GLOSSARY.MoE: Mixture of experts: selectively activate expert networks for each token.
GLOSSARY.Oracle: A reference computation or criterion that decides whether a property holds.
GLOSSARY.P99: The value at or below which 99% of measured samples fall; state the sampling boundary.
GLOSSARY.Prefill: Process known input tokens and build attention state.
GLOSSARY.Rank: One participant in a distributed process group.
GLOSSARY.RoPE: Rotary positional embeddings: a positional transformation of attention representations.
GLOSSARY.SLO: Service-level objective: a measurable target such as a latency percentile.
GLOSSARY.Softmax: Convert arbitrary scores to nonnegative probabilities summing to one.
GLOSSARY.SWA: Sliding-window attention: limit directly visible local key positions.
GLOSSARY.Teacher forcing: Feed a known continuation to compare model predictions on identical prefixes.
GLOSSARY.Tensor: A multidimensional array of numerical values.
GLOSSARY.TP: Tensor parallelism: split an operation/tensor across devices.
GLOSSARY.TTFT / ITL: Time to first token / inter-token latency. Specify queueing and delivery boundaries.
GLOSSARY.Weights: Learned numerical parameters defining the model’s calculations.
